newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine minister takes step towards presidency.
newsitem.headline: Philippine minister takes step towards presidency.

text.p: The Philippine Defence Minister, one of the least exciting but possibly leading candidates to be the country's next president, took the first major step on Friday toward entering the presidential race.

The Presidential Palace announced in a statement that Renato de Villa had been sworn in as a member of the ruling Lakas party, a necessary step if he was to win its endorsement to replace President Fidel Ramos in a year's time.

"I would like to thank the ruling party for the opportunity to participate in its worthy undertakings in the national interest and under the leadership of President Ramos," De Villa said in his low-key oath-taking ceremony.

Even though there are still 12 months to go, potential candidates have already been pushing themselves into the public eye in the hope of being chosen to lead the Philippines and its increasingly successful economy into the 21st century.
By far the most popular among voters appears to be former local movie star and the current vice-president Joseph "Erap" Estrada.
But his popularity among the masses is not matched in the business community where suspicion is strong that he lacks the intellect to keep the country moving forward.
Other known candidates include the economist daughter of a former president, who has teamed up with a former comedian, a cluster of senators and the present finance minister.

Ramos, who came to power in 1992, must quit next year under a young constitution which, mindful of the 20-year rule of the late-dictator Ferdinand Marcos, limits a president to a single six-year term.
De Villa's only real hope is if Ramos "anoints" him as his successor, analysts said.
The 61-year old former general has been called "Mr Wait-a-Minute" by Manila's media for a perceived slowness in making decisions, a tag he dismisses.
Described as a self-effacing man, he is also often called a Ramos "clone" because of supposed similarities in their leadership style and coincidental patterns in their careers.
The two men led loyalist forces in crushing six army coup attempts against then president Corazon Aquino.
